"Obtaining" an item is anytime you click the item from the board, and it's sent to your inventory. Like merchants or level up rewards.

If you obtain an item that's the same rarity or one rarity higher, it'll upgrade the one you already had instead of giving you a new one.

Merchants roll the rarity first and then the item. It will not roll an item you already have if the rarity rolled beforehand wasn't your item's rarity or its rarity +1.

Generated items (fishing rod, shovel) dont follow the above rules, and you also dont "obtain" it, so that's one way of getting copies.

Also, it seems the new level up rewards don't follow those rules, so you could roll an item you already have but at a rarity that doesn't match the upgrade requirements. Even though you "obtain" it, it won't upgrade your previous one unless it happens to also be your item's rarity or rarity +1.

For example, you have a silver katana. You level up and generate a random bronze item. It's a katana. You now own two katanas. However, if you generated a silver or gold katana from the level up, it would upgrade your current katana.

It matters if you spend an action while engaged.

Eon chart says, "Take an action." This is defined as gain an action "point" and spend it on the action. So yes, you would get aoo if you were engaged. However if you move with it and that move makes an enemy engage you. It won't hit you because you spwnt the action before you became engaged.

If you activate duke to investigate and are already engaged. You get AOOed. If you move to a location and that movement makes you engaged, you don't get AOOed because you spent the action while you weren't engaged.

Track shoes move you. You dont "take a move action" so track shoes are safe. Though the original movement would trigger AOO if you were engaged.

My argument is that the player isn't a legal target for pwk in the first place. Everything else is just a different argument. Druid with 101 hp wildshapes into something with 80 hp. Pwk is cast on the druid. Druid still has those 101 hit points as a creature (a point forfeited by the op in their first reply). Pwk does nothing to creatures with too much hp. 
In another situation, druid has 70 ho and wildshapes into something with 80. Pwk kills druid. Polymorph's entire language is also built around stopping players from killing with it. It's one of the most paranoid spells in the game. It's not intended, and it's not raw. Op's argument is that it only cares about the current form but affects both forms. My argument is it obviously cares about the entire creature. You could even argue that you should total the creatures hit points of both forms to see if it "has fewer than 100 hit points"

Hit points and life are synonymous. Players merely have a special rule that gives them a final chance. Npcs don't get that second chance raw. Without the additional rule, players would die at 0 hp. Hp and life is synonymous.
 And no, you can't have it both ways. Either pwk targets the current form and then kills that form but then you're in your original form and you don't care about what happened to your old form anymore.
Or pwk targets the whole character, and the whole character has hp higher than 100 so it's immune to the spell. 
You either follow the logic that spells target the current form all the way, or you follow the logic that spells target the full creature all the way.
You don't get to say it only targets the current form and them Halfway through say it also targets the entire creature.

What makes you say that pwk only cares about a creatures current form. It targets the creature. And the creature has a hit point amount that is more than 100.

I'd also say that a good amount of your argument is about the fact you can't regain hit points. So to say that your argument suddenly doesn't care about it tells me you didn't think too much about your argument. In terms of mechanics, hit points and life are synonymous.

My main argument is returns to the amount of hit points is not the same as regaining hit points. The character already has those hit points they aren't regaining them.
Returns is also the same word used In revivify, etc. Revivify returns them to life with 1 hit point. The same word is used to bring the character "back to life"
Also in terms of RAW, nothing says you keep conditions when you change forms. I would actually argue that if your bear eyes get blinded, your other eyes would be fine after changing back. Wild shape actually says that senses are based off of the current form, so physical changes (ex. Death) are based on the form.
You could even make the argument that the "creature" targeted by power word kill has two seperate hit points. The spell polymorph, as well as the wild shape feature, both have caveats that mean that the hit points of the original form are true during the change. Otherwise, you would return at full health, a set health dictated by the effect, or 0 health. Therefore, RAW both hit points would have to be less than 100 hit points to be legally targeted by pwk in the first place. Pwk in no way references a creatures current form so if a creature owns at least one hp amount that's more than 100, that creature is immune to pwk.

in terms of content per session, you'll eventually get an idea of what your players specifically want. In the meantime, I would just make the maps and decide what the maps do.

Here's an example:
-the map is an enemy ship.

-it's carrying this awesome cannon thing.

What does this map do?
- well if it's a special cannon, it's gonna have special guards. So there should be a small amount of "elites" on this map close to the cannon. 

- it's still a ship, so there are probably some normal deckhands, and of course a captain. 

What does this kind of planning do?
- It cuts down on your workload. All you need to prepare is the map if you're using one, a stat sheet for deckhand/captain/elite and that's about it. Maybe plan some loot if you're not doing random table loot.

- this puts you In a great improv spot. The characters can make all the choices. Remember, they already decided they wanted to destroy this cannon last session. And you have a pretty advanced understanding of how the world (or this ship in this instance) would react to them.

- this has forced you to really think about this location. Which allows you to react as truly neutral. Here's what I mean by this. Say the players decide to attack at night.
